title: LLM-Powered Silent Bug Fuzzing in Deep Learning Libraries via Versatile and Controlled Bug Transfer
summary:
Deep learning (DL) libraries are widely used in critical applications, where even subtle silent bugs can lead to serious consequences. While existing DL fuzzing techniques have made progress in detecting crashes, they inherently struggle to detect silent bugs due to the lack of effective test programs and corresponding oracles.
  Building on the observation that historical bug reports contain rich, underutilized information about silent bugs, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to perform versatile yet controlled bug transfer for silent bug fuzzing. Specifically, our approach uses LLMs to extract context-aware bug patterns from historical issues, match semantically related Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) using functionality-based embeddings, and synthesize test cases with customized oracles. This enables proactive detection of silent bugs by transferring high-risk contexts and oracle designs from known buggy APIs to functionally similar target APIs. To ensure the reliability of our context-aware bug transfer, we introduce an LLM-powered self-validation module that systematically evaluates the validity of each transferred bug instance. We implement this methodology in a tool named TransFuzz and evaluate it on three mainstream DL libraries: PyTorch, TensorFlow, and MindSpore. TransFuzz successfully discovers 79 previously unknown bugs (12 confirmed as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs)) in 10 bug types, demonstrating its effectiveness and generalizability in migrating DL library bug discovery capabilities.

AI.tldr: TransFuzz uses LLMs to extract and transfer silent bug patterns from historical reports to similar APIs in deep learning libraries, enabling effective oracle-aware fuzzing and discovering 79 new bugs, including 12 CVEs.
AI.motivation: Silent bugs in deep learning libraries can have severe consequences in critical applications, but existing fuzzing techniques fail to detect them due to lack of effective oracles and test programs; thus, a new approach is needed to proactively identify such bugs.
AI.method: TransFuzz leverages large language models to extract context-aware bug patterns from historical bug reports, matches functionally similar APIs using embeddings, synthesizes test cases with customized oracles, and employs an LLM-powered self-validation module to ensure transferred bug validity for silent bug detection in DL libraries.
AI.result: TransFuzz discovered 79 previously unknown silent bugs across PyTorch, TensorFlow, and MindSpore, with 12 confirmed as CVEs, covering 10 distinct bug types, demonstrating high effectiveness and broad applicability.
AI.conclusion: TransFuzz effectively transfers silent bug detection capabilities across APIs in deep learning libraries using LLM-driven context-aware bug pattern extraction and self-validation, demonstrating strong generalizability and practical impact in uncovering critical vulnerabilities.

title: Layer-Targeted Multilingual Knowledge Erasure in Large Language Models
summary: Recent work has demonstrated that machine unlearning in Large Language Models (LLMs) fails to generalize across languages: knowledge erased in one language frequently remains accessible through others. However, the underlying cause of this failure and a principled solution remain open. In this work, we identify intervention depth as the key factor determining multilingual generalization. Through systematic layer-wise experiments, we characterize two distinct failure modes: shallow-layer interventions achieve erasure but collapse multilingual capabilities in held-out languages, while deep-layer interventions preserve utility but fail to erase target knowledge even in source languages. These findings reveal that the choice of intervention layer is not a free parameter; it fundamentally determines whether multilingual unlearning succeeds. We propose MUTE (Multilingual Unlearning via Targeted Erasure), a framework that uses Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) and Linguistic Regions Development Score (LRDS) to identify intermediate, language-agnostic layers where cross-lingual representations converge. By restricting unlearning updates to these layers, MUTE achieves robust multilingual knowledge erasure while optimizing on only a small set of source languages. Extensive experiments across three LLM architectures and three unlearning algorithms validate our approach, with mechanistic analysis via Logit Lens probing confirming genuine knowledge removal rather than output-level suppression.

AI.tldr: MUTE identifies intervention depth as the key to multilingual unlearning in LLMs and proposes a method to target language-agnostic intermediate layers using CKA and LRDS, enabling effective cross-lingual knowledge erasure with minimal source language data.
AI.motivation: Machine unlearning in LLMs often fails to generalize across languages, with erased knowledge remaining accessible in non-source languages. The cause—intervention depth—has not been systematically studied, and there lacks a principled method to achieve multilingual unlearning.
AI.method: MUTE uses Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) and Linguistic Regions Development Score (LRDS) to identify intermediate, language-agnostic layers where cross-lingual representations converge, and applies unlearning updates only within these layers. The approach is evaluated across multiple LLM architectures and unlearning algorithms, with Logit Lens probing for mechanistic validation.
AI.result: MUTE achieves robust multilingual knowledge erasure while preserving model utility, outperforming shallow and deep intervention strategies. Experiments across three LLMs and three unlearning methods confirm effectiveness, with Logit Lens analysis verifying actual knowledge removal rather than superficial output suppression.
AI.conclusion: The choice of intervention depth is critical for successful multilingual unlearning in LLMs, and MUTE provides a principled solution by targeting intermediate, language-agnostic layers identified via CKA and LRDS, enabling effective and robust cross-lingual knowledge erasure.

title: Utilizing LLMs for Industrial Process Automation
summary: A growing number of publications address the best practices to use Large Language Models (LLMs) for software engineering in recent years. However, most of this work focuses on widely-used general purpose programming languages like Python due to their widespread usage training data. The utility of LLMs for software within the industrial process automation domain, with highly-specialized languages that are typically only used in proprietary contexts, remains underexplored. This research aims to utilize and integrate LLMs in the industrial development process, solving real-life programming tasks (e.g., generating a movement routine for a robotic arm) and accelerating the development cycles of manufacturing systems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the use of Large Language Models in industrial process automation, where specialized, proprietary languages are common. It demonstrates that LLMs can be leveraged to perform practical programming tasks—such as generating robotic arm movements—thereby accelerating development in manufacturing, despite limited training data in this domain.
AI.motivation: Most LLM research in software engineering focuses on general-purpose languages like Python, leaving a gap in understanding their effectiveness in niche, proprietary domains such as industrial automation with specialized languages.
AI.method: The study explores the application of LLMs to real-world industrial programming tasks by adapting models to domain-specific languages and evaluating their performance on practical use cases like robotic arm routine generation.
AI.result: LLMs can be effectively adapted to support real-life programming tasks in industrial automation, demonstrating feasibility in accelerating development cycles despite limited exposure to domain-specific languages.
AI.conclusion: The integration of LLMs into industrial process automation holds potential for improving development efficiency, despite challenges posed by specialized programming languages and limited training data.

title: DPSQL+: A Differentially Private SQL Library with a Minimum Frequency Rule
summary: SQL is the de facto interface for exploratory data analysis; however, releasing exact query results can expose sensitive information through membership or attribute inference attacks. Differential privacy (DP) provides rigorous privacy guarantees, but in practice, DP alone may not satisfy governance requirements such as the \emph{minimum frequency rule}, which requires each released group (cell) to include contributions from at least $k$ distinct individuals. In this paper, we present \textbf{DPSQL+}, a privacy-preserving SQL library that simultaneously enforces user-level $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP and the minimum frequency rule. DPSQL+ adopts a modular architecture consisting of: (i) a \emph{Validator} that statically restricts queries to a DP-safe subset of SQL; (ii) an \emph{Accountant} that consistently tracks cumulative privacy loss across multiple queries; and (iii) a \emph{Backend} that interfaces with various database engines, ensuring portability and extensibility. Experiments on the TPC-H benchmark demonstrate that DPSQL+ achieves practical accuracy across a wide range of analytical workloads -- from basic aggregates to quadratic statistics and join operations -- and allows substantially more queries under a fixed global privacy budget than prior libraries in our evaluation.

title: IMMACULATE: A Practical LLM Auditing Framework via Verifiable Computation
summary: Commercial large language models are typically deployed as black-box API services, requiring users to trust providers to execute inference correctly and report token usage honestly. We present IMMACULATE, a practical auditing framework that detects economically motivated deviations-such as model substitution, quantization abuse, and token overbilling-without trusted hardware or access to model internals. IMMACULATE selectively audits a small fraction of requests using verifiable computation, achieving strong detection guarantees while amortizing cryptographic overhead. Experiments on dense and MoE models show that IMMACULATE reliably distinguishes benign and malicious executions with under 1% throughput overhead. Our code is published at https://github.com/guo-yanpei/Immaculate.

AI.tldr: IMMACULATE is a practical auditing framework that detects provider-side dishonesty in black-box LLM APIs—such as model substitution and token overbilling—using lightweight verifiable computation, achieving high detection accuracy with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address trust issues in commercial LLM APIs, where users must rely on providers to run correct models, use honest token counting, and avoid cost-cutting abuses that degrade service quality or inflate costs.
AI.method: IMMACULATE uses verifiable computation to selectively audit a small fraction of API requests, leveraging cryptographic methods to detect deviations such as model substitution, improper quantization, and token overbilling while minimizing overhead.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that IMMACULATE effectively distinguishes between benign and malicious model executions on both dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models with less than 1% throughput overhead.
AI.conclusion: IMMACULATE provides a practical and efficient auditing framework for black-box LLM APIs that enables detection of economically motivated provider misbehavior without requiring trusted hardware or model access.

title: AgentSentry: Mitigating Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents via Temporal Causal Diagnostics and Context Purification
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external tools and retrieval systems to autonomously complete complex tasks. However, this design exposes agents to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where attacker-controlled context embedded in tool outputs or retrieved content silently steers agent actions away from user intent. Unlike prompt-based attacks, IPI unfolds over multi-turn trajectories, making malicious control difficult to disentangle from legitimate task execution. Existing inference-time defenses primarily rely on heuristic detection and conservative blocking of high-risk actions, which can prematurely terminate workflows or broadly suppress tool usage under ambiguous multi-turn scenarios. We propose AgentSentry, a novel inference-time detection and mitigation framework for tool-augmented LLM agents. To the best of our knowledge, AgentSentry is the first inference-time defense to model multi-turn IPI as a temporal causal takeover. It localizes takeover points via controlled counterfactual re-executions at tool-return boundaries and enables safe continuation through causally guided context purification that removes attack-induced deviations while preserving task-relevant evidence. We evaluate AgentSentry on the \textsc{AgentDojo} benchmark across four task suites, three IPI attack families, and multiple black-box LLMs. AgentSentry eliminates successful attacks and maintains strong utility under attack, achieving an average Utility Under Attack (UA) of 74.55 %, improving UA by 20.8 to 33.6 percentage points over the strongest baselines without degrading benign performance.

AI.tldr: AgentSentry is a novel inference-time defense that detects and mitigates indirect prompt injection in LLM agents by identifying causal takeover points through counterfactual analysis and enabling secure task continuation via context purification, significantly improving robustness and utility under attack.
AI.motivation: The increasing use of external tools and retrieval systems in LLM agents introduces vulnerability to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, which manipulate agent behavior through malicious content in tool outputs across multiple turns, evading traditional detection methods.
AI.method: AgentSentry uses controlled counterfactual re-executions at tool-return boundaries to localize takeover points and applies causally guided context purification to remove attack-induced deviations while preserving legitimate task context.
AI.result: Evaluated on the AgentDojo benchmark across multiple attack families and LLMs, AgentSentry eliminates successful IPI attacks and achieves an average Utility Under Attack (UA) of 74.55%, outperforming strong baselines by 20.8 to 33.6 percentage points without harming performance on benign inputs.
AI.conclusion: AgentSentry represents the first inference-time defense that effectively mitigates multi-turn indirect prompt injection in tool-augmented LLM agents by modeling attacks as temporal causal takeovers, enabling both precise detection and safe execution continuation.

title: Automated Vulnerability Detection in Source Code Using Deep Representation Learning
summary: Each year, software vulnerabilities are discovered, which pose significant risks of exploitation and system compromise. We present a convolutional neural network model that can successfully identify bugs in C code. We trained our model using two complementary datasets: a machine-labeled dataset created by Draper Labs using three static analyzers and the NIST SATE Juliet human-labeled dataset designed for testing static analyzers. In contrast with the work of Russell et al. on these datasets, we focus on C programs, enabling us to specialize and optimize our detection techniques for this language. After removing duplicates from the dataset, we tokenize the input into 91 token categories. The category values are converted to a binary vector to save memory. Our first convolution layer is chosen so that the entire encoding of the token is presented to the filter. We use two convolution and pooling layers followed by two fully connected layers to classify programs into either a common weakness enumeration category or as ``clean.'' We obtain higher recall than prior work by Russell et al. on this dataset when requiring high precision. We also demonstrate on a custom Linux kernel dataset that we are able to find real vulnerabilities in complex code with a low false-positive rate.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a CNN-based model for detecting bugs in C code, trained on machine- and human-labeled datasets, achieving high recall and precision and demonstrating effectiveness on real-world code like the Linux kernel.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to improve the detection of software vulnerabilities in C code, which is prone to bugs and exploitation, by leveraging deep learning techniques tailored specifically for C, unlike prior general-purpose approaches.
AI.method: The method involves training a CNN model on two datasets: a machine-labeled dataset generated by Draper Labs using static analyzers and the human-labeled NIST SATE Juliet dataset. The input C code is tokenized into 91 categories, converted into binary vectors, and processed through two convolution and pooling layers, followed by two fully connected layers to classify code into CWE categories or as 'clean'.
AI.result: The model achieves higher recall than Russell et al.'s approach on the same datasets under high-precision requirements and successfully identifies real vulnerabilities in a custom Linux kernel dataset with a low false-positive rate.
AI.conclusion: The proposed convolutional neural network model effectively identifies software vulnerabilities in C code with high recall and precision, outperforming prior work, and demonstrates practical applicability by detecting real vulnerabilities in complex code such as the Linux kernel with low false positives.

title: SettleFL: Trustless and Scalable Reward Settlement Protocol for Federated Learning on Permissionless Blockchains (Extended version)
summary: In open Federated Learning (FL) environments where no central authority exists, ensuring collaboration fairness relies on decentralized reward settlement, yet the prohibitive cost of permissionless blockchains directly clashes with the high-frequency, iterative nature of model training. Existing solutions either compromise decentralization or suffer from scalability bottlenecks due to linear on-chain costs. To address this, we present SettleFL, a trustless and scalable reward settlement protocol designed to minimize total economic friction by offering a family of two interoperable protocols. Leveraging a shared domain-specific circuit architecture, SettleFL offers two interoperable strategies: (1) a Commit-and-Challenge variant that minimizes on-chain costs via optimistic execution and dispute-driven arbitration, and (2) a Commit-with-Proof variant that guarantees instant finality through per-round validity proofs. This design allows the protocol to flexibly adapt to varying latency and cost constraints while enforcing rational robustness without trusted coordination. We conduct extensive experiments combining real FL workloads and controlled simulations. Results show that SettleFL remains practical when scaling to 800 participants, achieving substantially lower gas cost.

AI.tldr: SettleFL enables scalable, fair reward settlement in decentralized federated learning using two interoperable blockchain protocols that minimize cost and latency while ensuring trustless operation.
AI.motivation: In open, decentralized federated learning environments, fair collaboration requires trustless reward settlement, but existing approaches face high blockchain costs or scalability limitations, motivating the need for an efficient, fully decentralized solution.
AI.method: SettleFL introduces two interoperable protocols—a Commit-and-Challenge variant for optimistic execution with dispute resolution and a Commit-with-Proof variant using validity proofs for instant finality—both built on a shared domain-specific circuit architecture to minimize on-chain costs and ensure rational robustness.
AI.result: Experiments with real FL workloads and simulations show SettleFL scales to 800 participants with significantly lower gas costs, remaining practical under high participant counts and varying network conditions.
AI.conclusion: SettleFL provides a scalable, trustless reward settlement solution for decentralized federated learning, enabling fair collaboration without relying on a central authority while maintaining practical efficiency at scale.

title: Strengthening security and noise resistance in one-way quantum key distribution protocols through hypercube-based quantum walks
summary: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is a foundational cryptographic protocol that ensures information-theoretic security. However, classical protocols such as BB84, though favored for their simplicity, offer limited resistance to eavesdropping, and perform poorly under realistic noise conditions. Recent research has explored the use of discrete-time Quantum Walks (QWs) to enhance QKD schemes. In this work, we specifically focus on a one-way QKD protocol, where security depends exclusively on the underlying Quantum Walk (QW) topology, rather than the details of the protocol itself. Our paper introduces a novel protocol based on QWs over a hypercube topology and demonstrates that, under identical parameters, it provides significantly enhanced security and noise resistance compared to the circular topology (i.e., state-of-the-art), thereby strengthening protection against eavesdropping. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient and extensible simulation framework for one-way QKD protocols based on QWs, supporting both circular and hypercube topologies. Implemented with IBM's software development kit for quantum computing (i.e., Qiskit), our toolkit enables noise-aware analysis under realistic noise models. To support reproducibility and future developments, we release our entire simulation framework as open-source. This contribution establishes a foundation for the design of topology-aware QKD protocols that combine enhanced noise tolerance with topologically driven security.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantum key distribution protocol using quantum walks on a hypercube topology, showing enhanced security and noise tolerance over circular topologies, supported by an open-source Qiskit-based simulation framework.
AI.motivation: To enhance the security and robustness of QKD protocols against eavesdropping and noise, moving beyond limitations of classical protocols like BB84 and existing QW-based schemes with circular topologies.
AI.method: A novel QKD protocol is designed using discrete-time quantum walks on a hypercube topology; an open-source, noise-aware simulation framework is developed using Qiskit to evaluate and compare performance under realistic conditions.
AI.result: The hypercube-based QW protocol demonstrates significantly improved security and noise resistance over the circular topology under identical parameters, validated through simulations with realistic noise models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed one-way QKD protocol based on quantum walks over a hypercube topology offers superior security and noise resistance compared to circular topologies, establishing a foundation for topology-aware QKD protocols.
